claims.text: The initial refractory HEA is a homogenized, single-phase solid solution.
Rapid solidification minimizes precipitate formation in the initial alloy.
A post-solidification heat treatment will induce nucleation and controlled growth of nanoscale secondary precipitates.
The heat-treatment-induced precipitates may occur at grain boundaries or be dispersed within the matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitates pin dislocations and thereby raise yield strength.
Precipitates pin dislocations and thereby increase creep resistance.
Precipitates influence the elastic strain state and local stress distribution.
The precipitate-induced changes in elastic strain and local stress distribution mitigate the temperature sensitivity of elastic modulus.
Relative to the precipitate-poor baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the precipitate-poor baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have greater high-temperature creep resistance.
Relative to the precipitate-poor baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit a less temperature-sensitive elastic modulus.
The predicted property differences will be statistically significant.
The applicable service-temperature range is approximately 900–1200 °C under an inert or controlled atmosphere.
Severe oxidation or additional temperature-induced phase changes may limit the hypothesis.
The beneficial role of nanoscale precipitates in improving mechanical properties is supported in other alloy systems.
A controlled comparison can be made between identical samples receiving the precipitation-inducing treatment and samples retained in a homogeneous state without that treatment.

Failure of precipitate-rich samples to show statistically significant improvements, or observation of property degradation with increased precipitation, would falsify the proposed mediation hypothesis.
